title: When M.S. Subbulakshmi Sang at the UN, the World Stood Up. Sixty Years Later, 30 Artists in Dubai Are Singing It Again.
excerpt: A UAE-based collective of Indian classical performers reimagines the historic 1966 peace hymn Maithreem Bhajata — and the diaspora is listening
body:
When M.S. Subbulakshmi stepped up to the podium at the United Nations General Assembly in 1966 and began singing *Maithreem Bhajata*, delegates from across the world rose to their feet. The Sanskrit hymn — composed by the Paramacharya of Kanchi, Chandrasekarendra Saraswati — carried a message so elemental it needed no translation: cultivate friendship, conquer hearts, not nations.

Nearly sixty years later, in a Dubai studio thousands of miles from both Kanchipuram and New York, more than thirty Indian artists have breathed new life into that same hymn. Their production, titled *Mission Global Peace — Maithreem Bhajata*, brings together classical dancers, instrumentalists, and vocalists from across the United Arab Emirates in what its creators call "a unified expression of peace and harmony for a divided world."

## A Collaborative Effort Across Disciplines

The initiative is the brainchild of Guru Iswarya Bharadwaj, a UAE-based Indian classical dance teacher and performer who conceptualised and directed the project. Music direction came from Renuka Parameswar, while Varathraj Kumar of Ameeraga Valai Oli (AVO Studio) in Dubai handled the production. The result is a polished, multi-layered rendition that weaves Bharatanatyam, Carnatic vocal traditions, and ensemble instrumentation into a contemporary visual format designed for digital audiences.

The project has been presented jointly by the Global Indian Performing Arts & Music Society (GIPAMS) and IPF UAE. Since its release on 12 May 2026, the video has crossed 15,000 views and 1,500 likes across Instagram and YouTube, with shares spreading rapidly through Indian diaspora networks in the Gulf, Europe, and North America.

## Why It Matters Now

The timing feels deliberate. In a year marked by ongoing geopolitical tensions — from the Middle East to Eastern Europe — and with polarisation sharpening across democracies worldwide, the hymn's central exhortation to "seek friendship among all" strikes a chord that transcends its Vedic origins.

The UAE, home to an estimated 3.5 million Indians — the single largest expatriate community in the country — has increasingly positioned itself as a hub for cultural dialogue. From the BAPS Hindu Mandir in Abu Dhabi to the growing ecosystem of Indian classical arts academies in Dubai and Sharjah, the Gulf state has become an unlikely but fitting stage for Indian soft-power initiatives.

## The Original 1966 Moment

For NRIs unfamiliar with the backstory, the 1966 UN performance remains one of Indian music's most iconic moments on the global stage. M.S. Subbulakshmi, already regarded as the queen of Carnatic music, was invited to sing at the UN General Assembly — making her the first Indian musician to perform there. Her rendition of *Maithreem Bhajata* was received with a standing ovation, and the hymn was subsequently adopted into the UN's cultural archive.

The Paramacharya of Kanchi composed the hymn specifically for the occasion, drawing on the Vedantic concept of *vasudhaiva kutumbakam* — the world is one family. The Sanskrit verses urge listeners to abandon territorial conquest in favour of winning hearts through compassion and goodwill.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

Projects like *Mission Global Peace* serve a dual purpose for the Indian diaspora. They keep classical traditions alive and relevant in communities where the next generation often grows up more fluent in pop culture than in Carnatic ragas. But they also demonstrate that Indian cultural production abroad is no longer confined to temple festivals and community association galas. It can be slick, professional, and genuinely global in its ambitions.

Guru Iswarya Bharadwaj and her collaborators have shown that a classical Sanskrit hymn, born in a South Indian monastery and first heard at Turtle Bay, can find its third life in a Dubai recording studio — and from there, reach living rooms from London to Los Angeles.

## What's Next

The GIPAMS and IPF UAE teams have signalled that *Mission Global Peace* is not a one-off. The collaboration aims to continue producing cultural content that bridges Indian classical traditions with global audiences, leveraging the UAE's position as a crossroads between East and West. For a diaspora community that often struggles to transmit its artistic heritage across generations, that ambition alone is worth a standing ovation.
